extracted.intended_audience: cartoonists, humor writers, graphic-novelists, and literary writers looking for craft advice on using cartoonist techniques and large set-ups in longer works
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for creating cartoons (especially single-panel) and for adopting cartoonist principles—recognizable set-ups, twists, and scaffolding—when writing longer literary works or adaptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-panel cartoon structure: set-up and punchline
rubrics_metrics.description: A single-panel cartoon is a joke in drawing form: you start with a set-up, then add a punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the cartoon as a compact narrative built on a recognizable premise (set-up) that leads to a payoff (punchline). This is the basic unit of cartooning and humor-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a recognizable set-up
rubrics_metrics.description: The set-up has to be something most of your readers will recognize, so that they’ll get the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use common, culturally legible scenarios so readers bring shared knowledge to the gag. Examples New Yorker cartoonists rely on: desert island, cocktail party, therapist’s couch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a twist inside the set-up
rubrics_metrics.description: A set-up often contains a twist: there is a dog at the cocktail party, or the person stranded on the desert island is wearing skis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small incongruities within a familiar scene provide the surprise that makes a joke land; craft the twist to subvert expectations within the recognizable frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing the set-up is the hard part
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing the set-up is the hard part. Once you have your set-up in place, you can forget about structure and be purely creative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend effort deciding the premise; once the premise is solid, the rest of the creative play becomes easier. Avoid jumping to punchlines without a stable, resonant set-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a premade/expansive set-up to carry longer projects
rubrics_metrics.description: I’ve always wondered if it was possible to make a longer project more like a cartoon or joke. I thought that if only I could find a really expansive set-up, it would carry me along and keep me from falling into the horrific questions real novelists and graphic novelists have to ask themselves, such as What am I doing? and Why?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For long-form work, identify an expansive premise that can sustain many jokes, scenes, or thematic pivots so the author can focus on inventive details rather than constantly rethinking structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your source material when adapting
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem was that my target wouldn’t sit still. I realized I didn’t know the Old Testament (or Torah, as we call it) at all. It is a jumble of mysterious parts, some written centuries apart. I can’t summarize what it is trying to say.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before adapting or satirizing canonical or historical texts, thoroughly learn and understand the source; lack of familiarity will undermine adaptation and make the target unstable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a work that reads coherently at a distance while supporting stand-alone details
rubrics_metrics.description: You need to make something that can be seen at a distance as a coherent object and that a reader can enter as its own universe, full of stand-alone details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance macro-level coherence (an overarching object/shape) with micro-level, self-contained scenes or jokes so readers can both grasp the whole and enjoy discrete moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold dual perspectives: big-picture structure and intimate detail
rubrics_metrics.description: As a person who has trouble holding two ways of seeing in her mind at once, reading a book gives me the same kind of vertigo I get from trying to navigate using a map, or from contemplating my own mortality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate the ability to maintain both an overall structural viewpoint and close, moment-to-moment detail. This cognitive balancing is essential for creating layered work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid skimming the surface—build layers and multiple meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Even jokes and cartoons are complex stories with layers of history to them and multiple meanings. There is no such thing as skimming the surface. There is only the marvelous illusion of doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for depth: even seemingly light or comic material should contain historical layers, subtext, or multiple interpretive possibilities rather than being merely superficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use inventive character/conceptual twists to generate continuous questions
rubrics_metrics.description: As a personal twist, I decided to make my God female. I figured that would cause a continuous parade of interesting questions to arise in the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce a provocative reimagining (e.g., changing a canonical figure’s gender) to produce ongoing interpretive friction and fresh dramatic/comic possibilities; anticipate how perspective shifts will be read by readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor tone and voice to different story types within a larger work
rubrics_metrics.description: The first part of the project — the stories of creation, Babel, and Noah... was a pleasure to work on. What I came to think of as the second part of Genesis — the long, boring story of Abraham... was harder. I solved Abraham by telling his story like a Philip Roth book: a good book that was not written for me, a book with blind spots that are more apparent to me than others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that different episodes or source-material sections may demand different tones or narrative voices (comic, earnest, satirical, novelistic); choose approaches appropriate to each part rather than treating the whole uniformly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impose an overarching scaffolding to unify spliced-together texts
rubrics_metrics.description: I became a structure person. I created an overriding, earnest scaffolding to make sense of the spliced-togetherness of the text. I decided to make the story of creation take place in the past, Abraham in the present, and Jacob and Joseph in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting or assembling disparate materials, design an explicit organizing principle (timeline, framing device, thematic through-line) so the pieces cohere as a single work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let character arcs reflect structural choices (e.g., have God age)
rubrics_metrics.description: This led me to have God age throughout my story. From a child, she becomes a teenager, then a woman. She loses her innocent self-centeredness, becomes introspective. As she grows up, she stops being a cartoonist and develops a taste for story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use character development (aging, maturation, changing profession/temperament) to mirror and reinforce the work’s larger structural and thematic design.
